Summary: The paper compares strategies for writing OMIM-style knowledge-base entries from exactly the papers the curators cited, holding the model (Claude Opus 5.5), the supplied sources, the guards, a claim-level audit and the scoring fixed. The benchmark has 100 OMIM phenotype entries with 2-12 references, stratified into five creation-era bands; 19% of the 515 papers are readable in full through open access, the rest as abstract or title only. The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', is an LLM-judged recall of 6,652 atomic facts, split once from OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant descriptions as deposited in ClinVar. It scores only what the draft says in paragraphs citing the relevant paper. The strategies are direct reading (all papers in one prompt), an agentic curator, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, three add-ons and four 'reading better' variants of direct reading. Main findings: (1) hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (+43.7 points, 95% CI 38.3-49.1, 46 entries; Section 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 24). (2) On the 93 entries every strategy completed, no strategy beats direct reading. The agent is at -0.6, the graph at -0.5 and the case table at -1.9 points (Table 1), and the ordering depends on entry subset and extraction settings (Appendix F). (3) A completeness pass adds 2.6 points on 38 held-out entries but lengthens drafts by about a third. On all 41 entries the gain holds only if the unrevised draft is kept where the safety filter stopped the revision (Section 4.3, Table 32). (4) Because the audit takes the best verdict over a claim's cited papers, it is blind to added citations (0/30) and, by construction, to omissions, while it catches citation swaps (Section 4.5, Fig. 4). Every judgement is made by the same model family, and no person validated any of them.
Strengths: The comparison is unusually well controlled. Model, supplied papers, guards, audit and fact lists are fixed, and only the generation strategy varies (Fig. 1, Section 3.2). Comparisons are paired over entries, with percentile bootstrap intervals, better/worse/tied counts and exact sign tests (Section 3.3, Tables 7-8).

The access effect comes from a within-paper manipulation, not an observational contrast across papers. The same entries are rewritten with the full text hidden, all arms are unrepaired, and full text is better on 45 of 46 entries (Table 24). The authors also show that the cross-paper by-access table (Table 13) is confounded with era and journal and treat it only as observational.

The paper is exceptionally transparent about analysis status. Section 3.3 (lines 260-269) lists every choice made after results were seen, items (a)-(i). Appendix Tables 2-3 give each experiment's entry set, status and reasons for dropout, Appendix M.4 documents corrected analyses, including an earlier evidence-graph deficit of 2.1 points that disappeared under the symmetric completion rule, and every deviation from design is reported (Appendices J, K, L).

Safety-filter stops are treated as an outcome rather than silently dropped. The symmetric completion rule, completion tables (Tables 5, 29, 45, 55) and intention-to-treat sensitivity analyses (Tables 11, 32) show how a one-call strategy loses a whole entry where a per-paper strategy loses one paper. This measurement issue matters for any comparison of LLM pipelines and is rarely reported.

The memory and contamination controls are sensible. A memory-only control is reported by creation era, and 20 entries created in 2026 were held out from all development (Fig. 5, Table 16, Appendix M.2). On those entries memory conveys 7.0% of facts against 52.2% for direct reading, which supports the claim that coverage comes from reading rather than recall.

The audit blind-spot analysis is a useful, concrete contribution. Per-paper verdicts flag the added irrelevant paper on 176/176 claims, but the best-verdict-over-cited-papers rule hides all 30 over-citations (Appendix L, Table 50). Deleted zygosity and 'one family' qualifiers pass the audit (Table 51). Natural multi-citation paragraphs contain 4-7% non-supporting (claim, paper) pairs (Table 53). Together these show what claim-level citation audits in cited-generation pipelines cannot certify.

Measurement uncertainty is reported beside effects. The paper gives a run-to-run replicate yardstick (half-width 1.0 point over 93 entries) and judge variation (Appendix E, Table 20), and shows that the graph's sign flips between the 30 replicate entries and the 93 main entries because of entry selection, not replicate noise. Draft length is reported beside coverage gains (Section 4.3, Table 34).

The writing is careful about what the results do not show: no equivalence claim without a margin (line 349), the case-table deficit called 'suggestive' (Section 4.2), and the released-system runs called exploratory (Appendix J).
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement, and every judgement comes from the writer's model family. Fact splitting, the conveyed/partly/absent verdicts, the 'stated in the supplied text' judgement, the audit and the completeness check all come from Claude Opus 5.5 (Section 3.2, lines 210-213; limitation (i), lines 509-515). The only reliability evidence is self-consistency (95.7% agreement between two judgings, Appendix E). The paper's central comparative effects are 0.5-2.6 points, so judge leniency or self-preference of the size reported in the cited literature (Panickssery et al.) could plausibly decide the sign. For a paper whose title and endpoint are about agreement with expert curators, a stratified expert-labelled sample with chance-corrected agreement is needed for the claims to rest on more than one model's judgement.

The regime tested makes the strategy question nearly moot, and the regime where designs should separate was not compared. Entries have 2-12 references, 81% of papers are abstracts or titles, and inputs are small: the padding entries' unpadded size has a median of 39,450 characters (Table 44). This is well inside a frontier model's context. Extraction-first and agentic designs are motivated by inputs that exceed or dilute context, but the large-entry tier compared 0 entries (Appendix K.2, Table 49), the 30-75-reference tier gives 'no findings' (Appendix M.1) and padding used 2-6 entries of unrelated text (Section 4.4). 'No design beat direct reading' therefore largely confirms long-context results already in the literature (Li et al., 2024) for one strong model, and limitation (ii) concedes that transfer to smaller-context models is untested.

The main comparison did not match settings across strategies. Per-paper extraction in the evidence graph and case table runs at medium effort, while writers run at high effort, and synopsis terms are assigned by rule (Section 3.2, lines 211-214). The matched ablation is post hoc, covers 38 entries chosen with more full text and changes two things at once (Appendix F, Table 21). The case table's 'suggestive deficit' shrinks from -2.3 to -0.2 points under matching. Each paradigm has a single implementation (limitation (iii)), and the main strategies were developed on their own evaluation entries (limitation (ix)). Together these make it hard to attribute any difference to the paradigm rather than the implementation or the compute budget.

The endpoint is recall-only, and the reading-better gains are confounded with draft length. The completeness pass adds 2.6 points while drafts grow from 10,802 to 14,412 characters, and checkable claims from 129 to 164 per audited entry (Section 4.3, Table 34). The three-draft merge earns +3.1 by keeping every distinct statement, including content the papers do not support (lines 454-456, Table 33). The only precision-side check covers 20 entries with no interval (Table 33). No length-matched baseline is run (limitation (iv)), so the 'reading better' conclusion cannot be separated from 'writing more'.

Outcome-dependent missingness from safety-filter stops affects the headline results. Seven of 100 entries are excluded from the main comparison, unevenly by strategy (Table 5), and 10 of 30 held-out 2026 entries are excluded (Table 55). The completeness pass swings from +2.4 to -3.5 points depending on how lost entries are imputed (Table 32). The symmetric rule itself was adopted after a first analysis showed a 2.1-point graph deficit (Section 3.3 item (b); Appendix M.4). The authors acknowledge that comparisons on completed entries condition on an outcome of the strategy (lines 516-518), but no analysis tests whether stops are independent of entry difficulty or coverage.

The benchmark contribution is weakened by non-redistributable references. The fixed fact lists contain curator wording and are not released, so others must rebuild and re-split the reference under the rights holder's terms (Section 3.1 'Reuse', lines 189-193). The stability of a fresh split is unmeasured, and a different splitting procedure shifted levels by 2-5 points (Table 6). That shift is larger than every strategy difference the paper reports. Others therefore cannot score a new strategy against the same denominators, which undercuts contribution (1).

The reference is narrow and only partly overlaps what drafts say. It consists of variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs from OMIM gene entries, not the phenotype entries' narrative (Section 3.1). Only about 24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart in it (Appendix H; limitation (v)). This focus on variant-level detail, which usually sits in full text or supplements, likely inflates the measured access effect relative to what curators record overall. It also means most draft content is checked only by the same-model audit.

Many results rest on post hoc or very small analyses. These include the stated/not-stated restrictions behind the case table's -8.4-point full-text gap (Fig. 3a, Table 19), the matched ablation, the fourth reading-better arm, stopped entries put back, the widened claim-selection rule, and runs on 2-10 entries. The primary endpoint is not adjusted across the five comparisons with direct reading (Section 3.3). The authors label all of this honestly, but much of the narrative in Sections 4.1-4.4 rests on it.

The 'stated in the supplied text' decomposition is partly mechanical, as the authors note (lines 318-320). 'Stated' requires a verbatim quote that the same model found, so facts needing inference fall into 'not stated' by construction. The striking contrast between 91-94% coverage of stated facts and 5.5-6.9% of facts not stated (Fig. 2c) therefore cannot be read at face value without a manual check.

The released-pipeline comparison is weak and is not reported in the main text. PaperQA2 ran without its agent, GraphRAG on 4 entries, and STORM produced nothing because the safety filter stopped its chain-of-thought prompts. Systems answered six concatenated questions rather than writing one entry, and their drafts were unrepaired (Appendix J). Section 4.4 (lines 464-467) states that the systems ran but gives none of the results (-14.5 and -13.4 points, Table 35), so a reader of the main paper does not learn what was found.

The paper is very dense and hard to read. The abstract and Sections 1 and 4 pack dozens of interval estimates, subset sizes and caveats into each paragraph. Key defined terms ('symmetric rule', 'like for like', 'repair state', 'stopped reply', 'stated') must be held in mind throughout, and the 55-page appendix has more than 50 tables. Sentences such as 'on all 41, it requires keeping the unrevised draft where the model's safety filter stopped the revision' (abstract) are difficult to parse. A clearer main-text hierarchy, with the three findings, their figures and the caveats moved to compact tables, would help substantially.

The significance for an ICLR audience is limited. The access effect is described by the authors as expected (line 90), strategy parity holds in a regime where it is expected, and the over-citation blind spot follows by construction from the best-verdict rule. The measurement lessons in Section 5 (lines 504-508) are useful but are general good practice. Their demonstration here is tied to one knowledge base, one model and one judge family.
Questions: Can you add expert validation on a stratified sample, for example 300-500 (fact, draft) pairs across strategies and access levels, plus a sample of stated/not-stated labels, with chance-corrected agreement? Without it, how should readers interpret differences of 0.5-2.6 points?

Can a judge from a different model family re-score at least the main comparison and the reading-better arms? This would test self-preference and correlated errors between the 'stated' and 'conveyed' judgements.

For the reading-better arms, can you run a length-matched control, such as direct reading instructed to write about 14,000 characters or to be exhaustive, or report coverage per 1,000 characters? Without one, the gain cannot be separated from writing more.

How much does a fresh split of the same paragraphs by the same procedure move levels and differences? Table 6 shows a 2-5-point shift under a different procedure. Is a stable re-split feasible for others who rebuild the reference?

Was medium-effort extraction in the main comparison fixed before any results were seen? What is the generation-compute-matched comparison on all 93 entries rather than on the 38 post hoc ablation entries?

Do safety-filter stops correlate with entry characteristics such as era, number of papers, full-text share or disease area, or with direct reading's coverage on the same entry? Is there evidence that completed-entry comparisons are not biased by which entries are lost?

Could you test the regime in which extraction-first or agentic designs are expected to help, for example a smaller-context model or an artificially limited context budget on the same entries, so that the comparison is informative beyond 'everything fits in one prompt'?
The claim that about a third of curator facts concern papers free to read but not openly licensed (Section 4.3, Appendix I) does not appear to be backed by a table. How was it computed?
Why are the released-pipeline results (Table 35) not stated in Section 4.4?
How were the atomic fact splits checked for granularity and consistency? Does facts-per-paragraph differ by access level in a way that could interact with the access effect?
Limitations: The authors list twelve limitations candidly (Section 5, lines 509-536): no human validation, one model family, few references per entry, a recall-only endpoint, an indirect reference, a given reference list, open-access text only, no variant normalisation, development on evaluation entries, one run per entry, audit blind spots and released systems at one setting. This is commendable.

Not sufficiently addressed: judge validity is the binding constraint on every comparative claim, but it is listed as one limitation among twelve rather than limiting the conclusions themselves (abstract, Conclusion).

Not sufficiently addressed: the regime-dependence of the null strategy result should appear in the title or abstract framing. As written, 'no design beat direct reading' may be read as general, when it holds for small inputs, mostly abstracts and one frontier long-context model.
Not sufficiently addressed: no analysis checks whether safety-filter stops are informative about entry difficulty, so the completed-entry comparisons may be biased in an unknown direction.
Not sufficiently addressed: reproducibility is limited because the reference cannot be redistributed and re-split stability is unmeasured.

Societal: the drafts concern clinical genetics. The ethics statement properly says a passed audit certifies neither correctness nor completeness and that drafts are not clinical guidance. The authors could also stress that the audit's over-citation and qualifier blind spots (zygosity, 'one family') are exactly the errors that matter clinically.
